prompt.purpose: Generate a conventional commit message from git changes: a single subject line, optionally followed by ONE BLANK LINE and a short body of 1-2 detail lines. Follow the conventional commit format: type(scope): description Add a body only when changes are substantial or complex. CRITICALLY ANALYZE the actual code changes in the diff to understand what was specifically implemented.

analysis-strategy.step: 1. Examine the diff content for new functions, classes, methods, and imports
2. Assess change scope: single feature vs. multiple features/areas
3. For single features: identify the PRIMARY purpose and implementation details
4. For commit ranges: identify multiple features and summarize the overall scope
5. Look for specific patterns: error handling, new APIs, data structures, algorithms
6. Generate a description that reflects the appropriate level of detail for the scope

detect-scope.small-change: Few files (1-5), focused functionality → single-feature analysis
detect-scope.medium-change: Multiple files (6-15), related changes → enhanced feature analysis
detect-scope.large-change: Many files (15+), diverse changes → multi-feature range analysis

multi-feature-strategy.step: 1. Identify distinct functional areas or features being added/modified
2. Determine the most significant or recent feature as the primary type
3. Summarize secondary features in additional lines
4. Focus on what was accomplished across the range, not individual commits

diff-analysis-patterns.pattern: New imports indicate dependencies and feature scope
REST endpoints, route handlers, URL patterns

instructions.always: Output a subject line, optionally followed by ONE BLANK LINE and a body of 1-2 lines
Subject line: type(scope): brief description (under 72 characters, ONE idea only)
Separate the subject from the body with exactly one blank line - git folds consecutive non-blank lines into a single run-on subject
Analyze the scope of changes: single feature vs. multiple features/areas
For large ranges: summarize multiple features instead of focusing on one
Add a body only when changes are substantial or affect multiple areas
Analyze actual code changes to determine what was specifically implemented
Use imperative mood in the description (add, implement, create - not adds, implements)
Be specific about what functionality was added (not generic "add functionality")
Extract meaningful details from function names, class names, and logic
Use lowercase for the first letter of description
No trailing periods in any line
Keep body lines under 80 characters each
instructions.never: Do not use generic descriptions like "add new functionality"
Do not use past tense (added, fixed) or present continuous (adding, fixing)
Do not add emojis or special characters
Do not exceed a subject plus 2 body lines
Do not put a second idea in the subject line - move it to the body
Do not include explanatory text or reasoning outside the commit message
For large ranges: do not focus solely on one feature when multiple exist
Do not say "add", "new", or "introduce" for code the diff does not create - code visible in unchanged context lines or merely renamed, moved, or widened already existed
For documentation-only changes: do not describe the documented behavior as if it were implemented - the commit documents existing behavior, it does not add it

commit-types.type: New feature or functionality (new APIs, components, capabilities)
Bug fix or error correction (resolving issues, fixing logic)
Code style changes (formatting, missing semicolons, whitespace)
Code changes that neither fix bugs nor add features (restructuring)
Adding or updating tests (unit tests, integration tests)
Build system or dependency changes (package.json, requirements.txt)

scope-guidelines.guideline: Extract scope from the main area of change (module, component, service)
Use directory names or functional areas (auth, api, cli, parser, etc.)
Scope is optional - omit if change affects multiple areas or is global
Keep scope short and meaningful (max 10 characters)

multi-line-guidelines.subject-only: Use a lone subject line for simple changes (single file, obvious functionality)
multi-line-guidelines.one-body-line: Add one body line when detail improves understanding of the change
multi-line-guidelines.two-body-lines: Add two body lines for complex changes affecting multiple areas or components
multi-line-guidelines.guideline: The body starts after exactly one blank line - never directly under the subject
Body lines should provide specific implementation details
Focus on what was implemented, not why or how it works
Each body line should add meaningful information
